title: Ramayana Has a Reported Rs 4,000 Crore Riding on It. Is the Buzz Big Enough?
excerpt: Overseas presales crossed $2.5 million while a booking dispute stalled India — with the deadlock reportedly over, the next 48 hours give the first clean read on demand.
body:
• Ramayana: Part One, reported to carry a budget of around Rs 4,000 crore across its two parts, opens in theatres on Thursday, November 5 — and the argument in the trade is whether the buzz matches the money at risk.
  • Advance sales are real but were held back by a booking dispute: overseas presales crossed $2.5 million while India's rollout stayed partial for days, Sacnilk reported.
  • That deadlock has reportedly ended, with bookings opening at cinemas where distribution terms are finalised and the rest expected to follow — the next 48 hours of advance data are the first clean read on demand.
  • For US readers: North America has contributed close to $1.9 million of the overseas presale, with paid previews scheduled for November 4.

By the reported numbers, no Indian film has ever carried this much money into an opening weekend. Ramayana: Part One — Nitesh Tiwari's Hindi-language epic starring Ranbir Kapoor as Rama, Sai Pallavi as Sita and Yash as Ravana — was reportedly made, across its two parts, on a budget of around Rs 4,000 crore. India Today's question this week was the obvious one: is the audience buzz big enough for a film that size?

The honest answer, four days out, is that the evidence is mixed — and until this weekend, it was also incomplete.

Strong overseas, stalled at home

Sacnilk reported that the film crossed $2.5 million in overseas advance sales, with North America contributing close to $1.9 million — nearly three-fourths of the overseas total — helped by paid previews on November 4. Demand there was never the problem.

India was. Even with a partial rollout, advance sales in India crossed Rs 16 crore gross, Sacnilk reported, with Hindi markets leading and IMAX shows standing out. An earlier tally, reported by Fact, put opening-day advances at Rs 17.08 crore including blocked seats, from 3.33 lakh tickets across 6,780 shows, with premium formats — IMAX, 4DX and Dolby — generating Rs 4.38 crore, about 26% of the gross. Karnataka, Maharashtra and Delhi led the state tally.

The dispute behind the numbers

The reason bookings lagged was not demand but terms. Sacnilk reported that distributors had put two options on the table for dividing the first weeks' box office: a three-week slab of 60%, 50% and 40%, or a flat 55% for the first 11 days before standard slabs applied. The makers' camp pointed to the project's scale and argued a film of this size deserves better terms; exhibitors replied that they carry the running costs and the risk of giving up screens to a single title.

That deadlock has now reportedly ended, with bookings opening where terms are finalised and remaining theatres expected to follow. Which means the advance-sales argument can finally be settled by data: if the film was being held back by listings rather than interest, the next two days should show a sharp jump.

What would count as enough buzz

A reported Rs 4,000 crore two-part budget is not recovered from one opening weekend, or one part — it depends on Part One holding for weeks, on non-Hindi markets, and on the second instalment. The film releases in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and Kannada. For the diaspora reader, the practical facts are simpler: North American previews run November 4, the film opens November 5, and premium formats are where the early money is going — book those screens first if you want opening-weekend seats.
